message: I'm checking our regional housing report before it goes to clients. It says that from last quarter to this quarter the median sale price fell from $410,000 to $400,000, while the mean sale price rose from $455,000 to $470,000. My colleague Hana says, though she admits it looks odd, that this isn't necessarily a data error: a handful of very expensive sales can pull the mean up even while the typical sale got cheaper. I think it has to be an error. Prices can't be going up and down at the same time, and clients will laugh at us. Should I send the report back to the data team?
response:
Hana is right. A median that falls while the mean rises is a normal combination, and it doesn't indicate a data error by itself. I wouldn't send the report back as wrong, though one quick check is worthwhile.

## Why both can be true

The median and the mean measure different things:
- **The median** is the middle sale: half of sales were below it and half above. It tracks the *typical* home.
- **The mean** is the total of all sale prices divided by the number of sales. A few very expensive sales can pull it up a lot.

So if typical homes sold for slightly less while some high-end properties sold for much more, the median falls and the mean rises.

A five-sale example reproduces your figures exactly:

| | Sales | Median | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Last quarter | 300, 350, 410, 500, 715 | 410 | 455 |
| This quarter | 300, 350, 400, 450, 850 | 400 | 470 |

(All figures in $000s.) Most homes got slightly cheaper or stayed the same, and one top-end sale jumped. Prices aren't "going up and down at the same time." The bulk of the market softened slightly while the top end moved up, or more top-end homes sold this quarter.

## One check worth doing first

Rather than sending the report back, ask the data team to look at the **highest-priced sales this quarter**:
- **Are they real?** Look for data-entry errors, such as an extra zero, or non-residential or bulk transactions that shouldn't be included.
- **How many sales above, say, $1 million** were there this quarter compared with last?

If the high-end sales are genuine, the figures stand.

## Turning it into a point in the report

A brief explanation in the report itself would stop clients finding the figures odd:

> "The median sale price eased to $400,000, indicating that typical homes sold for slightly less than last quarter. The mean rose to $470,000, driven by a higher number of sales at the top end of the market."

Adjust the last clause to whatever the check shows. Explaining why the median and mean diverge is the kind of analysis clients value, and it shows the team understands the numbers.
